record.paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
record.original_question: For the explicit inductive growth algorithm of CTCS(n), in which one picks a uniform random bud, moves upward toward it, and either inserts a side-bud or extends the target bud into a new Exponential(1)-length branch, determine whether there exists a useful martingale that can be exploited to analyze the model.

evidence.quote: The growth algorithm. Given a realization of CTCS(n) for some n ≥ 1: • Pick a uniform random bud; move up the path from the root toward that bud.
Open Problem 13 Is there a useful martingale associated with the inductive construction?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the following family of random rooted binary trees with edge lengths, denoted CTCS(n) for integers n ≥ 1. The model is determined by the following discrete recursive splitting rule together with continuous-time edge lengths: for m ≥ 2, a clade of m leaves is split into two sub-clades of sizes i and m−i (with 1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability proportional to 1/(i(m−i)); each clade of m leaves is held for an Exponential(1/(m−1)) time before splitting (for m = 1 the leaf is held forever). The resulting random tree on n leaves with real edge lengths is CTCS(n).

The family (CTCS(n), n ≥ 1) admits an explicit inductive growth algorithm that constructs CTCS(n+1) from CTCS(n) as follows. Call each leaf of the current tree a "bud." Given CTCS(n):
 1. Pick a uniformly random bud and consider the path from the root to that bud.
 2. Move upward along this path; at each internal edge, with appropriate probability either:
    (a) insert a new side-bud (a new branch carrying a new leaf, attached at an interior point of the path with an Exponential(1)-length pendant edge), or
    (b) continue moving up; if the chosen bud is reached without insertion, extend the target bud by appending a new Exponential(1)-length branch terminating at a new leaf.
This procedure produces a sample of CTCS(n+1) and is consistent with the delete-a-random-leaf-and-prune dynamics on the family.

Question: Does there exist a nontrivial martingale (with respect to the natural filtration of this inductive growth process indexed by n) that can be used to derive quantitative information — for instance, fluctuation theorems or limit laws — about functionals of CTCS(n) (such as leaf heights, edge-length sums, or split statistics)?
artifact.status_search_result: The growth-algorithm martingale question appears in a list of open problems about the critical beta-splitting tree CTCS(n). Subsequent work (e.g., on harmonic descent chains, the exchangeable partition representation, and contraction-method analyses by Aldous, Janson, Pittel and collaborators in 2024–2025) develops alternative tools, but I found no source identifying an explicit "useful martingale" attached to the inductive growth algorithm itself; the problem appears to remain open.
